title: Mandala & Pattern Making
strapline: Petals, pebbles and buttons laid out in circles and rings — beautiful, temporary art built from pattern and symmetry.
intent: Children explore pattern, symmetry and rotation, working outwards from a centre in rings and repeats.
Children make deliberate aesthetic choices — this colour next to that, all the way round.
Children experience transient art: the beauty is in the making, and the piece can be swept away and remade.
Children sort and grade materials by colour, size and shape as they compose.
Children find calm, focus and pride in a slow, absorbing, open-ended activity.
implementation: Offer a round tray or a chalked circle and a palette of sorted natural and colourful loose parts.
Start a ring yourself sometimes — petal, pebble, petal, pebble — and leave it for a child to continue.
Talk about the centre and working outwards, and about matching one side to the other.
Provide mirrors and a camera so children can see the symmetry and keep the piece after it's gone.
Resist tidying too soon — let a mandala sit and be admired, and photograph it before it's swept.
Grade the challenge — simple two-colour rings for some, intricate graded spirals for others.
Draw out the aesthetic talk — which arrangement feels balanced, which colours sing together?
key_questions: What comes next in your ring — how do you know?
Does this side match the other side?
Which colours look beautiful next to each other?
Shall we photograph it before we tidy it away?
How could you make the pattern go all the way round?

impact.text: Children copy, continue and create patterns in rings and repeats and predict what comes next.
Children explore symmetry and rotation, matching one side of the design to the other.
Children make deliberate choices about colour, material and arrangement and own the result.
Children sort and grade materials by colour, size and shape as they compose.
Children stay absorbed in the slow, calming work and take pride in the finished piece.
Children place small parts precisely with careful, controlled fingers.

enhancements: Round trays, chalked circles and paper plates as bases.
Sorted palettes of petals, leaves, pebbles, buttons, gems and beads.
A large mirror tile under the work to reveal the symmetry.
A camera to keep each transient piece after it's swept away.
Books and photos of real mandalas, rangoli and natural patterns.
Graded challenge cards — simple rings up to intricate spirals.
A soft-music corner to make the pattern-making a calm retreat.

playing_exploring: Children explore colour, shape and arrangement freely, with no wrong answer.
They test how a pattern changes when they swap a colour or add a ring.
active_learning: The slow, absorbing work builds real concentration and staying power.
Children decide for themselves when the piece is finished and beautiful.
creating_thinking: Children predict and extend patterns and use symmetry to plan the next ring.
They make links between colour, balance and how a design feels.
